name: Israel Defense Forces in the Six-Day War (1967)

weightNotes.aggression: Pre-emptive war: Operation Focus struck the Arab air forces on the morning of 5 June, followed at once by the ground offensive; Tal's armour corps was trained for 'high mobility and relentless assault' (Operation Focus, Israel Tal pages; Oren, Six Days of War).
weightNotes.maneuver: Armoured divisions broke through and drove deep: Rafah was circumvented, the Sinai was taken and the Suez Canal reached within the six days (Six-Day War page; van Creveld, Sword and the Olive).
weightNotes.flanking: At Abu-Ageila Sharon's division landed paratroopers by helicopter to silence the Egyptian artillery in the rear while armour and infantry attacked at night (Abu-Ageila page); Rafah was bypassed. High.
weightNotes.siegePreference: No sieges: fortified localities were stormed or bypassed in a war of days. Near zero.
weightNotes.reserveUse: A mobilised reserve army committed almost entirely to three fronts in sequence, with the air force switched between them; little held back (Six-Day War page; Pollack). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Intelligence on Arab air bases made Operation Focus possible, destroying about 450 aircraft by noon on the first day (Operation Focus page). 1973's intelligence failure is a different era of this force, so 1967 rates high.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.coldwar high quartile 0.154. Sourced pressing through loss: no IDF withdrawal is recorded in 1967; paratroopers took Ammunition Hill trench by trench with 36 killed (Ammunition Hill page; Oren). Sinai 1967 is a backtest case and not evidence here. No measured share at withdrawal.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Abu-Ageila was a model night combined-arms attack (infantry, paratroopers, tanks, artillery), and air supremacy enabled air-ground support. But Tal's doctrine emphasised the tank, and that imbalance failed in 1973 when piecemeal armoured counterattacks were beaten by infantry anti-tank missiles (Abu-Ageila, Yom Kippur War pages). 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Commanders led from the front and exploited opportunities without waiting for orders; van Creveld (Command in War) uses the Israeli army as his modern example of decentralised command. Gonen entrusted the Rafah breakthrough to a single battalion (Six-Day War page).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: A short-war army: divisions drove to the canal on what they carried, with logistics improvised behind them (van Creveld, Sword and the Olive). Operations were not limited by supply planning in 1967. Low-middling.

summary: A small standing cadre and a large, quickly mobilised reserve army, fighting on interior lines against several neighbours. Doctrine stressed the pre-emptive offensive, winning air superiority first and then concentrating armoured divisions for deep breakthroughs, with commanders leading from the front and acting on intent. In 1967 the air force destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground by noon of the first day, then the army took Sinai, the West Bank and the Golan Heights in six days.
whyItWorked: Surprise and air superiority on the first morning (about 452 aircraft destroyed in Operation Focus), excellent long-range tank gunnery (Tal retrained gunners to hit beyond 1.5 km), and aggressive decentralised command against Arab armies whose junior officers showed little initiative (Pollack, Arabs at War). Abu-Ageila showed a well-coordinated night attack against prepared defences.
whereItFailed: Its 1967 success hardened into overconfidence in the tank and in intelligence: in October 1973 the surprise attack succeeded, and armoured counterattacks from 6 to 8 October were 'piecemeal and inadequately supported' and beaten by Egyptian infantry with RPGs and Sagger missiles (Yom Kippur War page). The doctrine depends on a short war, air supremacy and early warning; without them its small army was costly to sustain.
